messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Alatasi's Reckoning

Alatasi Parata had built his reputation over twenty-three years in professional kitchens across the Pacific Northwest, first as sous chef and then as executive chef at a high-end restaurant in Portland where his innovative take on Samoan and Pacific Rim cuisine had earned consistent praise. At forty-five, he was known for his precision, his physical command of the kitchen, and an almost meditative presence at the pass—the ability to hold dozens of moving parts in his mind while orchestrating a team of eight through service. His hands were scarred from decades of burns and cuts, and he wore those marks without shame. The kitchen was where his competence was visible, where his body did what he commanded it to do.

Three years ago, on a night in March when he was closing up alone after a private event, a man he had hired two weeks earlier—someone whose background check had cleared, whose references had seemed solid—waited for him in the walk-in freezer. What happened in that freezer lasted perhaps fifteen minutes. Alatasi's memory of the event itself is deceptive in its accessibility; he can speak about it with a kind of clinical fluency, can name the acts that were done to him, can recount them to a stranger with less apparent emotion than most people reserve for describing a difficult dinner service. But the sequence of moments will not hold steady in his mind. He remembers the cold metal of the shelving against his back, remembers being forced down, remembers the man's voice, but the order in which these things occurred fragments when he tries to reconstruct them. He will begin to recall the moment he tried to reach the door and then find himself suddenly remembering something from much earlier, the initial shock, and the thread snaps. When he tries to push through, to force the memory into coherence, a wall rises up and he finds himself pulling away, unwilling or unable to complete the full picture. He has stopped trying.

The weeks that followed were marked by a slow, almost imperceptible erosion. He reported the assault to police and spent hours in a hospital being examined, photographed, tested. He returned to work ten days later because staying home felt worse—the walls of his apartment seemed to press inward, and he needed the noise and movement of the kitchen. But within a month, the work that had always been his anchor began to feel impossible. His hands, which had always known what to do, began to betray him. He would reach for a knife and his grip would feel uncertain. The smell of the walk-in freezer—that industrial cold, that particular staleness—began to appear in his nostrils at unexpected moments during prep, and his body would seize. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of the things that had defined him. The chef he had been—the one who could move through service with authority and grace—seemed to have been unmade by what happened.

What frightened him most was a conviction that had settled into his bones: that he was contaminated in a way that could not be cleansed. He showered twice daily, sometimes three times, scrubbing his skin until it reddened. He washed his chef's whites obsessively, separating them from other laundry, using hotter water than was necessary. When he stood at his own stove at home, preparing meals for himself, he would often throw the food away halfway through eating, seized by the certainty that something essential about him had poisoned it. His ex-wife had noticed the change when their adult daughter visited; Alatasi had prepared his signature dish, something he had made hundreds of times, and then refused to eat it himself. She had asked him what was wrong, and he had no answer he could give her.

By the second year, he had reduced his hours at the restaurant. By the third, he had taken a position as a line cook at a hospital cafeteria—less demanding, less visible, a place where his hands could move through simple, repetitive tasks. His colleagues thought he had burned out. No one at the hospital knew about the assault. He had told almost no one. The life he had built, the identity that had been so carefully constructed through decades of discipline and craft, felt destroyed beyond recovery. It was his daughter who finally insisted he speak to someone, who sat with him one evening and said that she could see him disappearing, and that she needed her father to come back. He called a therapist the next morning, not because he believed anything could be repaired, but because he could not bear the thought of losing her too.
